title: Killers Of The Flower Moon - Mollie’s reaction?

commenti.body:
We do see her reaction from the peanut gallery in the court, no?  It's extremely understated and borders on unrealistic, but it's there. 

After my first viewing I was wondering why, with such a long run time, they had Ernest on the stand giving answers to questions the audience already knows.  

On subsequent watches, I realized it's because that's when it is all finally brought to light for Molly.

Lots of things unseen/unsaid in Killers: “Just because they don’t say anything doesn’t meant they don’t know everything.” So while it’s not stated, I don’t think that moment is about which of his crimes is the most evil or personal to her, it’s about her being able to trust him.

Yes he confesses in court to his part in the indirect killings of her sisters, that he was an accomplice but ultimately an unwitting one and didn’t get his hands dirty himself. He is judged by his peers and sentenced. This gives him atonement.

When Mollie visits him, it’s his final chance at absolution. For the first time they face each other with everything out in the open. Except she knows that’s not true. So I’m asking him what was in the medicine she’s giving him one final opportunity to be honest with her. He knows he’s lying, she knows he lying, but he still can’t bring himself to speak the truth because (I suspect) it was his one physical direct act of betrayal and it was to the person he loved the most. He couldn’t admit that he would do that to her because he doesn’t believe he would. It’s similar to shutter island in many ways imo.

I don’t know if Mollie was ever going to be able to forgive him anyway, but with that final lie she knows she can never trust him. He’s a coyote. Mollie is smart and she identifies this about him almost immediately, but she also knows he’s sincere when he tells her he loves her. This is why she allows him to keep giving her the medicine. I’ve seen criticisms of her character as being passive or even stupid to allow him to keep injecting her, but I think it’s more about her trusting Ernest. Her sister Minnie died of “wasting disease” most likely treated with the same poison she’s being given. The difference is that she insists her husband give the shot because he is the only person she can trust.

So yes, hiring a man to blow up your sisters house is pretty devastating, but I think it’s beautiful that the climax of this tragic epic film comes down to a lie between a husband and a wife.
Was Ernest an ‘unwitting accomplice’ to blowing up Reta’s house? Didn‘t he plot it (and maybe plant the explosives)?

Seems like an extraordinary oversight to ignore the reaction of our central character on learning that her trusted husband *murdered* her sister(s). 

Also bizarre that when she has a moment to confront him about it afterwards… she doesn‘t even mention it. Is she supposed to be a sociopath, too?

The comment you replied to just explained that we do see her reaction. In the court room. 

I think it's just in the character to maintain composure and try with all her might to be at peace with things she has no control over. It kind of parallels the peace and acceptance of something extremely difficult shown at the opening of the film with the Osage burying the ceremonial pipe and grieving the loss of their ways.

I wouldn't call him unwitting on that case, but he isn't the brain (King Hale is, and he is for all the murders) nor the executioner (Acie Kirby blows the house up) in Reta's murder. The only crime directly related to Mollie in which Ernest is more than the messenger between Hale and the killers is the poisoning of Mollie, as Ernest is the one giving her the shots.

Damn you watched it more than once? 

It was so bad though.
Ah OK. So what was Ernest’s involvement in killing Reta? He helped to implement it and absolutely knew that Reta was the target, right?
Of course! I got more and more out of it each time! Sorry you didn't like it

That's the theme of the movie. "Ignore the indigenous"

I can't even begin to tell you how predictably bad this movie was. Within the first 10 seconds of it starting, I knew it was going to be the Forrest Gump of whatever type of movie it was trying to be. 

You're asking why the movie didn't really show Mollie's reaction.  Well, honestly, Scorsese had 3.5 hours to tell a story, and he decided to show the Osage as people as 3 things: drunk, ignorant, or dead.  They got represented for maybe 12 minutes throughout the whole movie and only in the presence of DeNiro and DiCapprio.

The worst part is Scorsese's self-indulgent monolog at the end of the movie. God, what a shitty ending. He had one more chance to let someone from the Osage get a final word, get to actually say something about what happened. He chose to do the opposite. That dudes lack of awareness is glaringly pathetic.

I dont know. 

It just strays from the actual story in very weird ways. I know quite a bit about what happened with regards to this topic and I think it glossed over so much. It also just wasn't very compelling of story writing. It really was a pretty superficial movie, there wasn't anything shrouded in mystery or nuance.

Really? I actually read the book Killers of the Flower Moon two summers ago and I thought the movie was jam packed with information and told pretty much everything from the book that I can remember.  

What exactly did you feel was missing, may I ask?

I thought it glossed over and outright left out some very important details. 
Congress, the FBI, the systemic guardian system, corruption of so many government officials. It was just really bad storytelling. It barely scratched the surface of any of that and decided to focus on mollie and earnest. And again what was with Scorsese's monolog at the end?  
Basically the whole movie was sorely predictable and superficial to me. And to also just blow over what happened to Hale was silly as well. I mean You have 3.5 hours to tell a story and this is how you choose to do it?  It was just mind blowing to me thats all. And very boring.
I'm sorry, I just don't feel the same way whatsoever
That's cool. It ain't that big of a deal. Can I ask, is Killers of the Flower Moon the only book you've read about the subject, or the systemic approaches to indigenous people?
Yes, I think it is. If you have any good recommendations, I do read a lot.

No, don't do that. 

I mean it isn't that big of a deal that we disagree. 

Just Google it. And just start with one written by someone indigenous, that's always a good start.
But I really do read a lot....do you know any good books?  I love books
Well, how did you find KOTFM?

You could start at the beginning. 

I'd read Columbus by Laurence Bergreen. 

Although not an indigenous person, it's definitely a good start because he is a decent historian, and most other books are gonna completely white wash the shit out of Columbus.
I heard that it was being made into a movie by Martin Scorsese

The "self-indulgent monologue" *ought* to feel cheap.

After 3 hours, the idea of everything we witnessed being communicated to a bunch of gormless radioheads *should* repel us. 

The possibility that all the suffering could *actually* be captured in something as cheap and trite as a radio stage play where all the murdered indigenous women are voiced by a single white voice actress *should* seem pathetic.

By seeing the stark difference between what we just saw, and the facsimile Scorsese shows us on stage, he hopes we realize the impossible gap between the prior three hours and the historical reality of the Osage's suffering. 

>He had one more chance to let someone from the Osage get a final word, get to actually say something about what happened. He chose to do the opposite. That dudes lack of awareness is glaringly pathetic.

He did. What's the final shot?

Mollie tells Ernest of that dream she has where they put all of his secrets in a box then got rid of the box and went off together. She was willing to let him come clean and start over. Because she really did love him. 

Except at the very end when she asks about the medicine. He’s too ashamed to tell the truth. And she’s too angry to give him any room for error.

In reality, Mollie did initially stand by Ernest and say how much she loved him. But very quickly became disgusted and wanted nothing to do with him. 

[Full breakdown](https://filmcolossus.com/killers-of-the-flower-moon-2023-explained)

Yeah if I gotta be honest the only thing I did not enjoy in that film was her acting. I mean the character just goes through waaay to many changes in mood to the point where it just seems unnecessary, she goes from being smug to being sad, then happy, then sick, then healthy again, and finally what just killed the character for me was her reactions through the hole trial. Even when Ernest sorta confesses to poisoning her and plotting to kill her sister she just stands there with a blank expression.

I noticed that too, and I think a lot of people did, but I actually liked the understated reaction, whereas the obvious one is to GO BIG. I wonder if they had big takes, and decided to use this. Mollie is a stoic personality and they chose to depict her as extremely an strong woman, even when faced with great grief and horror. There is an unknowable mystery to their relationship, where you think she must know more than she admits and is in some kind of denial about it to maintain her relationship. And we wonder how much Ernest truly loves her, as it's implied that he does indeed love her, but he's an idiot and a son of a bitch who betrays her again and again.

I think part of the context that is missing in the film is that the real-life Mollie had suspected that her husband was poisoning her and admitted as much to her priest. This scene is extremely briefly included in the film where Mollie is sitting in an empty church with a (oddly overacting) priest sitting right next to her - although in the film she doesn't explicitly say as much, just that she is afraid at home and he asks why she is afraid in her own home. I strongly suspect that there was more to this scene and they chose to cut it down. In reality, she suspected Ernest much longer and more directly. But her divorce from him followed the same timeline.

One of the things I liked about this film, and I like about films in general, is when people act in defiance of logic or reason. I guess it's frequently frustrating and confusing, but I don't think characters should always be understood, and like in reality, people make all sorts of poor decisions or rationalizations that don't make any sense. I think this film did a good job exploring that about their relationship, that makes no sense, and yet there is a lot of passion there.

She was being drugged with improper medications including heroin, that's why she became bed ridden and depressed. Then she sat through a trial hearing unspeakable horrors and had no way to process that. The emotional devastating wouldn't be something easily emoted by most people; they would be numb.

I agree with your point that a large part of the problem for the Osange is that they couldn't trust anybody. She puts miss placed hope in her husband because there is simply nowhere else to put it.

But I also agree with OP that the framing was curious at times. The scene where Ernst tells her he is going to recant on his testimony against Hale and she just nods was perplexing to me in the theater. By this point it is obvious Hale masterminded the entire thing and Ernst defending him is too much of a betrayal in that moment to play the way it did on screen IMO. At least not without me scratching my head thinking I missed something.

She *forgave* him for murdering her sister?

Is she insane?

If my wife was Margot Robbie and I learned that she‘d been murdering my family I’d kill the evil bitch. This guy ain’t no male Margot, he’s a low IQ dufus.

If you love your spouse so much that you can look past them murdering your family then you are mentally ill to a terrifying degree.

If my wife was Margot Robbie and I learned that she‘d been murdering my family I’d kill the evil bitch. This guy ain’t no male Margot, he’s a low IQ dufus.

I didn’t say it was a great call lol. Just that that’s what the movie sets up. She seemingly would have been willing to move past it if he had totally come clean. 

It bothered me a lot too and made her come off as silly. One of the reasons I don’t rate the movie as highly as others.

Haha! My dear husband, you’ve been secretly murdering my entire family but if you come clean I’ll be able to ‘move past it’ 🤣

That just makes Mollie look utterly insane. The film really needed to show her reaction to learning that Ernest was slaughtering her family. Way too big of an omission to leave it out.
A couple of downvotes from offended sociopaths would be expected, but we’re currently on 19. WTF is wrong with you people??

My (admittedly very limited) understanding is that in real life, Mollie believed Ernest was innocent and  tried to argue that her husband was incapable of doing such things. She slowly came around later.

In the film, I think it plays up more she has SOME suspicion of Ernest, especially in that one scene right before he surrenders himself for arrest. You can see it in her eyes that she wants to believe him…but can’t do so completely anymore.
